title: Ahead: the summit
hookLine: year five reads the source texts slowly and builds your own lasting practice

cards: Near the top of a mountain, the trail changes. The trees thin out. The steps get steeper and slower.

And for the first time on the whole climb, you can turn around and see the valley you came from: the switchbacks, the stream you crossed, the place you nearly turned back. Then you turn again and look up.
The top is close enough to see now, and still not close enough to touch. The day after tomorrow, this path begins its fifth year, and the outline has a name for that year: the summit.
Today is a look up the slope before the last climb.

teach.b: Year five opens with short sacred texts read whole: the Dhammapada, the Psalms, the Sermon on the Mount, the Bhagavad Gita, the Quran, the Japji of Guru Nanak, the Heart Sutra, the Analects, Ecclesiastes and more.
Each belongs first to the people who keep it, so the year begins by learning to read as a guest.
Second, walking with the poets: Rumi again, Hafiz and Kabir, Tagore, haiku, George Herbert, Hopkins, Wordsworth and Blake, Whitman, Dickinson. Not a survey. Companions for the walk.

Third, building your own practice. The year turns from reading to making: a daily practice, a weekly one, the seasons of a year and of a life, what to do when it breaks, and at the end, writing your own rule.
That's where yesterday's honest list comes in. You build from what you already do, not from a wish. Fourth, a line from the end of Walden.
Henry David Thoreau wrote: "If you have built castles in the air, your work need not be lost; that is where they should be. Now put the foundations under them."
Four years of thinkers, questions and schools have built a good many castles in the air. Thoreau doesn't ask you to knock them down. He asks for foundations.
And a summit isn't where the mountain ends. You still walk down. What changes is the view you carry with you.

how: People following a long course of study often pause before its final stage to look at what's ahead and choose one practice they mean to keep through to the end.

practice: Bring yesterday's list to mind and look at it the way a climber looks back at the valley: this is how far it came.

Then, gently, look up, with no plans and no promises, and ask one quiet question: which of these would I like to carry all the way to the top? Let one rise a little above the rest, and if you pray, you can hold it in prayer.
